title: Preparing for Practice Period
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the early Zen stories of Bodhidharma and his student Huike as the six-week winter practice period approaches. Nomon tells of Huike standing in the snow outside Shaolin until buried to the waist, then reads three exchanges, including the advice to have "no coughing or sighing in the mind." Stories from a mindfulness class for veterans at a Seattle VA hospital, where some find relief only on their motorcycles, sit alongside a visit to the Seattle Soto Zen group. Nomon closes by sending the room into groups of three to ask when adding effort to practice helps and when it becomes another failed resolution.

sentences.text: Good evening everybody.
Well, I have a potpourri of things that I'd like to share with you tonight, and I'm hoping to be brief and have some discussion time.
I'm hoping the result of my miscellaneous remarks will be to bring up the practice coming up, a practice period.
Maybe you don't know, and maybe you all do know, we have every year a six-week period in the winter of more something practice.
I was going to say more intensive, but it might not be more intensive.
I don't know what the right adjective will be for you, but more something.

In a monastic establishment, it would be pretty obvious to everyone what to do, because they would write a schedule that would be more rigorous than the usual schedule, with more meditation and study and classes and so on.

We do that to a limited extent, but basically we recognize that most of us don't have, wouldn't be possible for us to all come to the dharma hall two or three times more often or do a whole bunch more practice together.
So for us the challenge of practice period is to sort out for ourselves what that time should be for me.
How should I work with that in my home practice, in my coming to the dharma hall?
And just in how I approach my day, and approach each moment of my life during those six weeks.
So I'm hoping to bring up the topic of intensive practice.
Or is there any word you use that's easy to sort of overdo?
More serious practice?
More committed practice, more gentle practice, more firm practice.
I don't know what it will be.

I want to update you about miscellaneous things and then hopefully have a discussion to prepare us a little bit so we can be thinking about this, because next Thursday we'll have the opening ceremony, so a week from tomorrow, I think.
Yeah, a week from tomorrow.
You ready for this?

In no particular order, I wanted to mention a practice I'm doing for practice period, which is that I've started an eight-week apprenticeship in Seattle, going to a mindfulness-based stress reduction class for veterans at the Veterans Administration Hospital on Beacon Hill, which is south Seattle too, which is really far.
Seattle's not just one place, it turns out.
They're pretty spread out.
I've only been one time.
The classes are every Thursday morning, so my plan, which I hope I can sustain, is to go down on Wednesday night.
So if I book out of here the second we're done, that's why I won't really want to chat.
I went to one class, and the people who come to the class, most of them are veterans.
A few of them are staff members of the VA.
Almost all of them are veterans.
About half of them are exactly what you would imagine: big guys in their maybe middle 60s with tattoos and motorcycles.
We shared a little bit of our stories of why we were coming to the class.
It was heartbreaking to listen to these big guys, but it was pretty much what you would expect.
They'd been through a lot.
Several of them said they had us do things in the military that nobody should have to do.
They have chronic pain, some of them pretty constantly.
And mostly life just feels like too much.
Life is a little too intense all the time.
They've tried a lot of things: official medication and unofficial medication and everything in between.
And these guys are really willing to try meditation if they think it might help.
Mindfulness-based stress reduction, MBSR, is essentially meditation in different forms.
Pretty simple, with an emphasis on mindfulness of the body.
Anyway, these guys are pretty much what you would expect, about half of them.
One thing I learned which really shifted my attitude is the motorcycle thing.
I've always been a little scornful of these big guys zooming around on their big motorcycles.
Maybe you have too.
But one of the questions that we asked them was, when are you relaxed?
When's the time that you are relaxed?
Several of them said, "I don't know if I'm ever relaxed."
But several of them also said, "The one time I'm relaxed is zooming down a two-lane highway on my shovel nose," or something.
They had terms on motorcycles.
There's a feeling of intensity and control and freedom to them riding their big motorcycles.
Riding their big motorcycles is one of the few times that they have some relief from suffering.
I want to mention that because now I'm much more sympathetic to motorcycles.
But the other half of the people in the class were not what you would expect.
Quite a few were women.
Many were younger.
Several have received injuries.
Several of them are quite mild-mannered looking people, but when they spoke, you could tell that they were wound up inside tighter than a really tight spring.
Several of them said, "It's unusual for me to say anything out loud about how I'm feeling, but I'm doing it anyway.
I'm usually too angry to do that."
So anyway, that's one of my practice period jobs.
Also several of them said they actually have been interested in meditation for quite a while, but they've always been sort of intimidated and afraid to do it.
These don't look like the kind of people that you usually see come into meditation halls.
So it seems really good that they're developing a way to bring meditation, bring this sense of mindfulness and presence, acceptance, spaciousness, to people where they are.
They don't have to come here.
We can go there to where they are.

A lot of what doing this class reminds me of, and also another time when I got to teach meditation to the Christians at Samish Island, and another time teaching meditation to the people with multiple sclerosis that Nancy did too, I'm impressed in a very deep way with how powerfully healing simple awareness is, simple mindfulness of what's happening right now, just breathing, just being quiet.
It's so simple.
I think as we get into the religion business, we get a little busy with all the other things, and it's easy to lose contact with that basic powerful simplicity of simple mindfulness.
This is really something that we can all re-investigate and reaffirm and re-explore during practice period.
What if we were more able to slow down a little bit and just be present and see what that is?
Not worrying about things as much, not trying to figure things out as much, not trying to do things as much, but just practicing being.
So anyway, working with these different groups has given me a lot more appreciation because I can see the difference.
One hour, two hours of practice, and people who have never been anywhere near a meditation hall are really feeling some benefit, really shifting.
Another thing I wanted to mention, and I don't know why I'm doing so many things at once: I went down to the Seattle Soto Zen group on Sunday.
They invited me to go down and give the Dharma talk there, and it was really lovely.
They meet in a very nice Aikido dojo just across the ship canal from Fremont, so it's pretty central and easy to get to.
There's parking, and it's at a pretty easy time, Sundays at 9:30.
So if you're ever in Seattle, it's well worth going.
The [unclear: "forum"] is pretty much exactly what we're doing.
It's a different group of people, with some little differences, but it really is so encouraging.
It gives you more confidence, I think, in practice to go to other practice places and say, oh, it's not just some weird thing that we're doing in this particular location in Bellingham.
It's something much more universal and much broader.
So I recommend visiting them, and the group in Vancouver.
Groups are springing up everywhere within this everyday Zen family style.
Laurel Vogel is trying to start a little group on Whidbey Island.
There's a group on Salt Spring Island, a group on Cortez Island, far to the north.
You'll meet some of the people from Seattle.
I was inviting them to come, and many of them said they wanted to come here, and hopefully we can start going there.
That's another way that we strengthen and encourage each other.
You'll also meet the priest who's working with them, Echo Jeff Kelly, who has been up here before and was at Samish last year.
I invited him to come to practice period, and he's going to come to the one day sesshin on February 13th.
I've been talking to Jeff about some collaborations too.
Maybe we'll do sesshin together with the Seattle guys.
That'll be fun, and there are a lot of things we can do.
When I was there, I was trying to figure out what to say.
It's hard to figure out what to say at a Dharma talk.
Jeff said that they had been studying Bodhidharma, the famous, iconic, sort of mythical first ancestor of Zen in China.
These early ancestors of Zen, I've always had a hard time relating to them.
Maybe you have too.
They're so iconic and so intense.
At first they seem so one-dimensional, just a screen onto which somebody projected some intense, rigorous idea of Zen.
So I thought I would re-investigate a little bit Bodhidharma and his successor, Huike.
Some of this material I put in the [unclear: "responding gate"] email that you might have already seen.
I sent it today.
As part of my talk, I investigated some stories about Bodhidharma and Huike to see if there was something more to this than I had understood before.
What's obvious right away about these stories is the intensity of their enthusiasm for practice.
I don't know if you know these stories, but there are all kinds of stories about how intense Bodhidharma was.
And then Huike, his student, had already been practicing, I didn't realize this, for quite a while, 10 or 12 years, and had important enlightenment experiences and visions.
We would be happy to have Huike, before he met Bodhidharma, show up and teach us.
That would be great.
I didn't realize that.

Then through a combination of visions and advice from his teachers, Huike heads down to Bodhidharma's place, Shaolin Temple, which I think is sort of a shack on the edge of a cliff or something, with a cave in back.
I don't think it was a very impressive place.
The story is that he knocked on the door, and Bodhidharma wouldn't let him in.
The back story you have to remember with these is that he probably had walked for a few weeks to get there, because China is a big place and there's no transport.
And it was December, so Huike just stood there.
There's a tradition still in Zen monasteries of doing this.
When you're going to enter a training at a formal Zen training monastery, you go up to the Han, like we have, you whack it really hard, three times I think, and then you just stand there and wait.
They ignore you for a couple of hours or a day maybe.
Eventually somebody shows up and takes you to the waiting room, and then there's a whole other process that takes a while.
But you just stand there.
You don't say, excuse me, look around, call ahead, or have your credit card ready or anything like that.
So Huike was just standing there in the depth of winter, and of course it starts snowing, and he just stands there all night as it snows until he's buried to his waist.
This is the incredible enthusiasm these guys have.
And then it gets worse.
Bodhidharma consents to talk to him, basically, okay, so what do you want again?
Huike explains he wants to study the way.
Bodhidharma says something along the lines of, even if I told you, you wouldn't understand it, and shuts the door again.
Then there happened to be a very sharp sword lying around.
I don't know why there's always a sharp sword lying around when you need it.
In the snow, yeah.
It couldn't be usual for a monk to have a sharp sword, I don't think, but who knows, maybe he had it with him.
And then the story, which we can take metaphorically, is he chops off his left arm, says this is his left arm, and then Bodhidharma says, oh, okay, you're actually serious.
Okay, well, come on in, you can sleep over there, start training.
Of course, he probably wouldn't survive that.

But even though that is probably just a metaphor, monks and nuns have, up to the present day, in some small but steady numbers, practiced bodily mutilation as an [unclear: "aesthetic"] practice, usually cutting off a finger.
I don't know anyone directly, but I know people who know people who have done this practice, if you want to call it that.
So religion is pretty strange, isn't it?
Even one based on the relief of suffering can inspire some extreme action.
But then I kept reading and thinking about this, and I realized there's more to the stories than just extreme practice.
Here are two teachings that are recorded between Bodhidharma and Weka.
After eight years of practice, so this is full time, sitting a good chunk of the day, studying, working, probably they had to beg for their food.
It's not really recorded how they lived exactly.
Maybe people from the nearby village brought them offerings.
But probably pretty simple, intense practice.
*Eight years into this, Weka asked Bodhidharma, "Can I hear about the seal of truth of the Buddhas?"
And Bodhidharma answers, "The seal of truth of the Buddhas is not received from another."*
The seal of the truth of the Buddhas is not received from another.
It's really a powerful, humble interaction, isn't it?
First is Weka just having the courage to ask that question.
After eight years of serious study, wouldn't you be a little embarrassed to say, "So what does this mean again?
What's the point of all of this?
I think I missed that"?
I think we would mostly just be too embarrassed, and we'd probably slink off in the night, or just keep slugging along and hope that we'd figure it out.
So it's very humble on the part of Weka to ask that question: what does this mean?
And Bodhidharma's reply at first might seem not too helpful in a way: I'm not going to tell you.
But actually, if you think about it, it's also quite humble, and deeply supportive of his student.
You can't get this from somewhere else, from somewhere outside.
Rely on your own heart.
And I'm here.
I'm here to support you, but I can't solve this for you.
I can't tell you any magic answers.
You have to surround this exchange with the context of living intimately together for eight years.
Can I hear about the seal of truth of the Buddhas?
The seal of truth of the Buddhas is not received from another.
It reminds me of a famous attitude in Bodhidharma, from the Buddha's day on.
And it also reminds me, Dogen has a wonderful expression that the family jewels don't enter through the front gate.
So don't be looking out there somewhere for the family jewels.
You had them all along.
You just forgot.
You didn't notice what they looked like.
There are many allegorical stories in Buddhism making that point.
But there are lots of ways that you can understand or misunderstand these kinds of teachings and exchanges.
I think it's a misreading to think that this kind of exchange means the teacher has nothing to offer and it's all on the student.
There's an implied intimacy, and just unlimited, unconditional support in the presence and kindness of a good teacher and a good sangha.
To have people in your life who are willing to just be there, even though they don't have any answers for you.
To just be there steadily and patiently, ready to help, no matter what, no matter who you are, what you think you understand or what you don't think you understand.
So I'm starting to realize these early Zen stories have a lot of that in them, intimacy and support.
In another time, Bodhidharma gave Weka this teaching on how to practice.
*Bodhidharma instructed Weka, "Outwardly cease all involvements.
Inwardly have no coughing or sighing in the mind.
With your mind like a wall, you can enter the way."*
*Outwardly cease all involvements.
Inwardly have no coughing or sighing in the mind.
With your mind like a wall, you can enter the way.*
I just love that little thing about coughing and sighing.
Don't you hear what he's saying there?
It's a sense of, and it can be very subtle, these subtle layers of resistance and avoidance of what's actually happening.
In the context of formal practice, they can be quite obvious, because you actually do that.
The first period or two of zazen is fun, but then the third or the fourth one, there can be a little coughing and sighing in the mind, a little complaint.
The first half is important too.
Don't overdo it in your interactions with the external world.
Don't get too busy.
Don't get too crazy.
You have some control there over how involved you are.
We might think, "Yeah, but they were monks and it works for them, but I'm a little too busy for that."

I think all of us have a little more control and a little more choice than we think we do, both in the actual apparent circumstances of our life and in the ways in which we engage and get involved with those circumstances.
That might be something also to study during practice period.

You probably still have to go to work just as much during those six weeks, but you might be able to engage with those circumstances in a different way, with the quality of ceasing, the quality of spaciousness.
I thought that was very loving advice from Bodhidharma to Weka.
Here's one more, one last one.
If you want to read these again, they're all in your email.
This relates a little bit to our shuso, I guess, because it's about hiking, the teaching about hiking.
*One time Weka climbed up [unclear: "a few houses peak"] with Bodhidharma.
Bodhidharma asked, "Where are we going?"*
Whenever you hear "Where are you going?" or "Where are you from?", it's a Zen question.
Where are we going?
*And Weka said, "Please go right ahead.
That's it."
Bodhidharma said, "If you go right ahead, you cannot move a step."
Hearing this, Weka was greatly enlightened and had a real feeling of awe.*
So this is another intimate interaction from a thousand years ago on the other side of the planet, about seeing the potential for awakening in every moment, in every action.
Hiking along together, but still considering, what is this?
What is this?
What is this walking?
What is this place?
What is this body?
What is this?
And being willing to challenge the other person's assumption about the reality of their living.
You might think that you are a person who is walking and getting somewhere, doing something in your life.
A person over here with a goal that's over there.
But maybe with that attitude, you're not going to get anywhere really.
Maybe there's potential for real liberation if you can let go of all of your plans.
Don't try to go right ahead.
Just take a step.
Anyway, this little text goes on to describe a few more qualities of their practice, a few more qualities of Weka's career.

And it says in there, and who knows if any of this happened historically, but it still is great, it says that instead of establishing some kind of temple or monastery, Weka moved to the capital and lived there as a homeless person, just teaching and helping out where he could.
It says that he would teach at wine shops and butcher stalls, which is a little scandalous, alcohol and meat.

And it said that he would work with the outhouse cleaners, work with the outhouse cleaners, which I think means going along with a cart and a shovel, and going to each house or each business and shoveling the shit out of their outhouse, putting it on the cart, taking it out to the farms.
I was reading actually a contemporary account of Zen training in Japan, and that was one of the jobs.
They didn't have flushed toilets.
They would shovel out this shit and take it to a farm.
A very detailed description about how they would balance the buckets and how you had to go pretty fast because you didn't have much time, but not too fast.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Have you read that?
Oh, you met him, huh?
Chiryu.
Chiryu.
Yeah, so you met that guy.
Yeah, great book.
Worthy to talk about his experience.
I one time got to do that.
I learned a lot about aversion.
It's a great practice to shovel shit.
So anyway, back to Weka.
So, real humility, a real commitment to ongoing training.
He wasn't there just spouting off his mouth.
He was there studying his mind, helping out as best he could.
And maybe that way of living was Weka's response to Bodhidharma's instruction to cease all involvements and have no coughing or sighing in the mind.
And finally, the story talks about radically accepting whatever circumstances arise in our life, and, being a Zen story, it's a bit extreme.
So it says that at one point, Weka was teaching outside the gates of a fancy temple and drawing a pretty good crowd.
And the priest of the temple inside was upset by this, as you would be.
What's that guy doing?
Probably pretty scruffy.
And so he denounced Weka as a heretic to the authorities.
China for thousands of years has been fabulous about rules and bureaucracy, right?
And what you're not supposed to do, you do the wrong thing, and they shoot you.
And that's what they did.
Weka was arrested and executed.
And the story goes that he did not resist or make a fuss or try to defend himself.
I suppose he only had one arm.
It's hard to get away.
It's implied that it was obviously futile.
The authorities were convinced by the respectable other priest.
So why make trouble?
I think it would be a misunderstanding to say that one should be passive in the face of injustice.
So anyway, as winter practice period comes, I thought it'd be worthy to consider together some of these qualities from these old Zen stories.

See, are there ways that we can put these teaching stories to use, to not think that these are fables, not really real, or that these were sort of superhuman people who are better than us, that we could never practice as deeply as them?
But it's sad to just see what we can learn, how we can re-engage our life creatively with these stories of intimacy, humility, courage, creativity, and most of all, just steadiness.
Ten years, twelve years, twenty years, thirty years, steady practice.
And so what I thought we would consider together in small groups, I think groups of three, is: what has been your experience to date when you try to add something?
Do New Year's resolutions work?
Is adding something, or trying something new, or trying to do something more strenuously, when is that helpful?
Is there some quality or a way in which you approach it that makes it more likely that it'll be useful to you?
Or when is taking on anything extra just a disaster, just another failure, another screw up, another time you tried something and couldn't follow through?
And maybe we could, ahead of practice period starting next week, think a little bit about how I can apply effort in a way that will benefit myself and others, so I don't just set myself up.

Sometimes in the opening ceremony we invite people to go around and everybody says their plan, and there's always, and it might well be me or you, but there's always one or two people who make this outrageous plan, you know what I mean?
I'm going to sit three times every day, I'm going to study this, this, this, and this, I'm going to work on this practice, I'm going to never raise my voice in anger.
So one can overdo it, but one can also underdo it.
One can also act from fear and memories of past failures and trouble and not have confidence that you can actually change your life.
You can live in a different way with a different attitude and a different approach.
It's very possible to do that for six weeks.
For one thing, you have the support of Sangha.
Everybody else is making the same commitment, with the support of the schedule at the Zendo and the retreats at the beginning, middle, and end of the time.
Those are greatly supportive.
You can make a few of those.

But what's tricky about it, and in a way our lay practice is quite a bit harder, I think, than the monastic practice, where everything sort of worked out for you, is we've got to figure out how to add this to our life as it is, all of our other obligations and habits and tendencies.
How can we create a little more space for practice and engage this in a positive way?
All right, does that seem like a worthy thing to bring up?
So, could you please spread around the room and find yourselves two partners, so, group of three, and just sit together, and then I'll give a little more instruction about what to do next.
And it's fun if it's somebody you don't know so well, too.
I don't know if we have a number divisible by three, but we'll soon see.
And you've got to be not too close to the other groups so you can hear each other, so just use the whole room.
